title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: the promise and the proof

questions.prompt: A hotel advertisement printed these three promises, and no others: "You'll be met at the airport." · "Every room has a shower." · "There are excursions every day." Which complaint is built on something the advertisement really promised?

options.text: You said that we would be met at the airport, and we waited there for two hours.
You said that every room had a sea view, and ours looked onto the hotel car park.
You said that the excursions were free, and we paid for every one of them.
You said that the hotel had a swimming pool, and it was closed all week long.

questions.explanation: A complaint is only as strong as the promise it reports, and the manager will have the advertisement in front of him. Being met at the airport was promised, and nobody came: the report is faithful and the complaint holds. A shower in every room is not a sea view. Excursions every day is a promise about how often they run, not about their price. And a swimming pool was never mentioned at all. Reporting more than was promised is the quickest way of losing an argument you were winning.

questions.prompt: A manager writes down what his receptionist told him on Tuesday: "She said that she had sent the confirmation the day before and that she would call the airline that afternoon." Which words did the receptionist actually use?

options.text: I had sent the confirmation the day before, and I would call the airline.
I sent the confirmation yesterday, and I will call the airline this afternoon.
I have sent the confirmation today, and I am calling the airline now.
I will send the confirmation tomorrow, and I called the airline early this morning.

questions.explanation: Reading a report backwards means undoing every move: would comes forward to will, the day before comes back to yesterday, that afternoon to this afternoon, and the reporter's she becomes the speaker's I. The past perfect had sent could come from a past simple or from a present perfect, and it is the time marker that decides: the day before points to yesterday, so the original was sent, not have sent today. Copying the report's own tenses inside quotation marks reports nobody's words, and swapping the two verbs reverses the order of the events.

questions.prompt: Marion's letter of complaint mixes two kinds of sentence. Tick EVERY sentence in which she reports a promise the agency made — not a fact about her holiday.

options.text: You told me that the price included all the airport taxes.
We arrived at two in the morning after a nine-hour flight.
You said that the hotel would be finished before the season.
The building site beside the pool started work at seven.
You promised us a room with a view of the sea.

questions.explanation: A reported promise always shows the same two marks: a reporting verb whose subject is the agency (you told me, you said, you promised) and, behind it, words that somebody else once pronounced — included and would be finished are the backshifted forms of includes and will be finished. The two other sentences have no reporting verb at all: they are Marion's own account of what happened, and they belong to the second move of a complaint, where you state the facts. A complaint needs both kinds, but only the promises can be held against the agency.

questions.prompt: At the desk, the agent answers a complaint: "I do apologise for the transfer, madam. But I have your booking form here, and the excursions were never part of your package." What is the agent doing?

options.text: he apologises for both complaints and offers a refund
he rejects both complaints and blames the customer
he apologises for one complaint and rejects the other
he accepts both complaints but refuses to pay anything

questions.explanation: One answer often makes two moves at once, and the hinge is the word but: everything after it is what the agency is refusing. The apology covers the transfer, and only the transfer; the booking form is then produced as evidence that the excursions were never sold with the package, which rejects the second complaint entirely. Nothing in the answer offers money back, nobody is blamed for anything, and an agent who accepted both complaints would not be reaching for the paperwork.

questions.prompt: A guest said at the desk: "I am not leaving this office until somebody refunds my money." Which report tells the reader HOW she said it?

options.text: She insisted that she would not leave until her money was refunded.
She admitted that she would not leave until her money was refunded.
She apologised for not leaving until her money was refunded.
She denied that she would leave until her money was refunded.

questions.explanation: Say and tell report the words; the other reporting verbs report the force behind them, and choosing the right one is what turns a transformation exercise into real writing. To insist is to hold your ground and refuse to give way, which is exactly what staying in an office until you are paid amounts to. To admit is to accept an unpleasant truth about yourself, and she is claiming a right, not confessing anything. To apologise is the opposite move. And to deny is to say that something is not true, whereas she is announcing what she will do.

questions.prompt: The agent offers: "We can't refund the trip, but I can give you a 20 % discount on your next holiday with us." Marion answers: "I'm afraid I won't be booking another holiday with your agency." What does her answer mean?

options.text: she accepts the offer but wants to pay even less next time
she refuses the offer, because it is worth nothing to her
she is asking the agent to explain his discount once again
she apologises for having complained about her holiday

questions.explanation: I'm afraid announces a polite refusal, and the rest of the sentence explains why the offer is empty: a discount only lowers the price of a trip you are going to take, so a discount from an agency she will never use again is worth exactly nothing. Refusing compensation is not haggling over its size, and nothing in her answer asks a question. As for the apology, I'm afraid looks like one but is not: it is the standard English cushion under a piece of bad news.
